name: Ishtar Gate
info: The Ishtar Gate was the eighth gate of the inner city wall of Babylon, built c. 569 BCE by order of King Nebuchadnezzar II and faced in blue glazed bricks; its smaller frontal gate was later rebuilt in Berlin.

facts.made: Built on the orders of Nebuchadnezzar II of Babylon, who dedicated it to the goddess Ishtar; its glazed bricks were pressed, fired and glazed by Babylonian brickmakers
facts.form: A double gate of glazed brick, 15 metres high with foundations extending another 14 metres underground, faced in blue with low-relief dragons, aurochs and lions, and carrying a 60-line Akkadian cuneiform inscription
facts.where: The site is at Babylon, near present-day Hillah in Iraq; the reconstructed smaller frontal gate stands in the Pergamon Museum in Berlin, and panels are in many other museums
facts.known: blue glazed bricks meant to represent lapis lazuli; reliefs of mušḫuššu dragons, aurochs and lions; the Processional Way and the New Year procession; Nebuchadnezzar's dedication inscription; its reconstruction in Berlin; the debate over its return to Iraq

t: Nebuchadnezzar II had the gate built c. 569 BCE on the north side of Babylon and dedicated it to Ishtar; it opened onto the Processional Way used for the New Year procession of the gods.
Its bricks were pressed in moulds, fired, glazed in blue to imitate lapis lazuli and sealed with bitumen, and the façade carried rows of dragons, aurochs and lions.
The German excavation under Robert Koldewey sent most of the gate and the Processional Way's lions to Berlin, and Iraq has petitioned for its return, notably in 2002 and 2009.
dyk: Each of the lions along the Processional Way was made of forty-six moulded bricks in eleven rows, and of the 120 lion friezes on the street the German excavators took 118.
ev: Nebuchadnezzar II ordered the gate built on the north side of Babylon
Claudius Rich's topographical records of the ruins of Babylon, the first ever published, appeared
Robert Koldewey began his part in the excavation of Babylon
The excavation, which had uncovered 14 metres of the gate's foundation, came to an end
After the First World War ended, the smaller frontal gate was reconstructed in the Pergamon Museum in Berlin
A smaller reproduction of the gate, built under Saddam Hussein, was completed in Iraq
The government of Iraq petitioned Germany to return the gate, and petitioned again in 2009

sections.origins:
The Ishtar Gate was the eighth gate to the inner city wall of Babylon, in the area of present-day Hillah, Babylon Governorate, Iraq. It was constructed c. 569 BCE by order of King Nebuchadnezzar II on the north side of the city, as part of a grand walled processional way leading into the city. Nebuchadnezzar II reigned 604–562 BCE, the peak of the Neo-Babylonian Empire, and is known as the biblical conqueror who captured Jerusalem. He dedicated the gate to the Babylonian goddess Ishtar.

In the dedication inscription the king calls himself the first born son of Nabopolassar, King of Babylon, and says that the two gate entrances of the city walls, Imgur-Ellil and Nemetti-Ellil, had become increasingly lower after the street from Babylon was filled. He pulled down these gates, laid their foundations at the water table with asphalt and bricks and had them made of bricks with blue stone on which bulls and dragons were depicted. The gate was only one small part of the design of ancient Babylon, which also included the palace, temples, an inner fortress, walls, gardens, other gates and the Processional Way. The lavish city was decorated with over 15 million baked bricks, according to estimates.
sections.content:
The original structure was a double gate, with a smaller frontal gate and a larger and more grandiose posterior section. The gate was 15 metres high, and its foundations extended another 14 metres underground. There were three primary entrances: the central one held the double gate structure, with two sets of double doors for a fourfold door structure, and doors flanked it on the left and right. Its roof and doors were made of cedar, according to the dedication plaque.

The walls were finished in glazed bricks mostly in blue, with animals and deities in low relief at intervals. Alternating rows of mušḫuššu dragons, aurochs and lions symbolised the gods Marduk, Adad and Ishtar. Marduk, the national deity and chief god, appears as a dragon with a snake-like head and tail, the scaled body of a lion and powerful talons for back feet. Adad, who had power over destructive storms and beneficial rain, is shown by his sacred animal, the aurochs, a now-extinct ancestor of cattle. Linear borders and rosettes, often seen as symbols of fertility, completed the design. The Processional Way that ran through the gate was lined with walls showing about 120 lions, bulls, dragons and flowers on yellow and black glazed bricks, with crenelated buttresses along both sides.
sections.making:
The bricks were made of finely textured clay pressed into wooden forms, and each animal relief was made from bricks formed by pressing clay into reusable moulds. The seams between bricks were planned so as not to fall on the eyes of the animals or on other unsuitable places. The bricks were sun-dried and then fired once before glazing, and in this bisque-fired state the clay was brownish red.

The background glazes are mainly a vivid blue that imitates lapis lazuli, a deep-blue semi-precious stone revered in antiquity. Gold and brown glazes were used for the animals, and the borders and rosettes were glazed in black, white and gold. It is believed that the glaze recipe used plant ash, sandstone conglomerates and pebbles for silicates, melted, cooled and pulverised into a frit, with colour-producing minerals such as cobalt added to the final formulations. The glaze was painted onto the bisque-fired bricks and fired at a higher temperature. After this firing the bricks were assembled with narrow horizontal seams of one to six millimetres, sealed with bitumen, a naturally occurring black viscous substance like modern asphalt. A wood and clay gate glazed to look like lapis lazuli could possibly refer to the goddess Inanna, who became syncretised with Ishtar and who, in the myth of her descent to the underworld, is described as lapis lazuli, silver and wood.
sections.reception:
Once a year the Ishtar Gate and the connecting Processional Way were used for a New Year's procession, part of a religious festival celebrating the beginning of the agricultural year. In Babylon the rituals of this holiday lasted twelve days. They began immediately after the barley harvest, at the time of the vernal equinox, on the first day of the month of Nisan. Statues of the deities were paraded through the gate and down the Processional Way. The purpose of the festival was to affirm the supremacy of Marduk and his representative on Earth, the king, and to offer thanks for the fertility of the land.

The Processional Way, traced to a length of over 800 metres, was designed with reliefs of lions, the symbol of Ishtar, the dragon of Marduk and the bull of Adad. Ishtar, also known as Inanna, was worshipped as the Mistress of Heaven and was the goddess of war and the protector of ruling dynasties and their armies. Friezes with sixty lions decorated each side of the way, with variations in the colour of the fur and the manes. In the 19th century Claudius Rich, British resident of Baghdad, published the first topographical records of the ruins of Babylon, in 1815; he and most other visitors thought a mound there was a royal palace, which Robert Koldewey's excavations later confirmed.
sections.survival:
Koldewey, a German excavator, took part in the excavation of Babylon from 1899 and led the work until 1914; during it 14 metres of the gate's foundation were uncovered. The method then favoured by the British, tunnels and deep trenches, damaged the mud brick foundations, but the recording of data was far more thorough than in earlier Mesopotamian excavations. Walter Andrae, Koldewey's assistant, was an architect and draftsman who documented the site.

The German Oriental Society had provided large funding, and the German archaeologists felt they needed to justify the cost by smuggling much of the material to Germany. Of the 120 lion friezes on the Processional Way the Germans took 118. The pieces were disassembled by a numbering system, packed in straw in coal barrels to disguise them, shipped down the Euphrates to the Shatt al-Arab and loaded onto German ships for Berlin. There hundreds of crates of fragments were desalinated and pieced together with new bricks fired in a specially designed kiln. The smaller frontal gate was reconstructed in the Pergamon Museum after 1918 and stands 14 metres high and 30 metres wide; the larger rear part was considered too large for the museum and is in storage. Panels and animals are also in museums in Istanbul, Copenhagen, Detroit, Gothenburg, Munich, Vienna, Toronto, New York, Chicago and Boston, and in the Louvre.
sections.legacy:
The acquisition of the Ishtar Gate by the Pergamon Museum is surrounded by controversy, since the gate was excavated as part of the excavation of Babylon and shipped to Berlin, where it remains. The government of Iraq has petitioned the German government to return it many times, notably in 2002 and 2009. The gate is frequently used as an example in the debate over repatriating artefacts of cultural significance to countries affected by war, and over whether such pieces are safer in another country. In the gate's case the question concerns its safety after the Iraq War, and whether it would be safer at the Pergamon Museum, where it was damaged by bombs in the Second World War.

Under Saddam Hussein a smaller reproduction was built in Iraq as the entrance to a museum that has not been completed; it was completed in 1987, with the purpose of reconnecting to Iraq's history, and it has been damaged since the Iraq War. The façade of the Iraqi embassy in Beijing includes a replica of the gate, and those in Amman and Islamabad evoke it. In 2011 a joint Italian-Iranian team found at Tol-e Ajori, near the Achaemenid capital of Persepolis, a monumental gate with similar plan and decoration, with glazed brick fragments showing the same aurochs and mušḫuššu motifs, dated to the mid-to-late sixth century BCE.

summary: The Ishtar Gate was built c. 569 BCE by Nebuchadnezzar II as the northern entrance of Babylon, faced in blue glazed bricks with dragons, aurochs and lions. German excavators took most of it to Berlin, where the smaller frontal gate was rebuilt, and Iraq has asked for its return.
notes: The article gives Koldewey's excavation as 1904 to 1914 in the lead and 1902 to 1914 in the excavation section, and says his part began in 1899; the text gives 1899 to 1914 and leaves out the other two start years.
Construction date c. 569 BCE from the lead; the inscription's date is given as around 605–562 BCE, left out.
The article says the gate 'depicted only gods and goddesses' yet describes rows of dragons, aurochs and lions as symbolising the gods; the text keeps the symbolising wording.
The article's Processional Way is said to be lined with about 120 lions, bulls, dragons and flowers, and also to have sixty lions on each side; both are given as the article gives them.
The reconstruction date: the lead says it came after 1918 without a year; the event is labelled 1918 with 'after the war ended'.
The sole reference listed in the article (Matson 1985) is the editor's to add if wanted; references left empty as instructed.

The article uses the word smuggling for the removal and says the excavators felt they needed to justify the cost; the text gives this as the article does, and Iraq's petitions are given without a verdict.
